passage: I'm Jagdish, and for two years my mornings belonged to the chat window. Every ping pulled me out of my code, and by lunch I had written very little. Last spring I changed one rule: I read messages at eleven and at four, and at no other time. I told the team. Indu, who leads our group, asked, "And if it's urgent?" I said, "Call me." I muted the chat and closed the tab. The first days were itchy; I kept wanting to check. But by the second week I was finishing the hard parts of a feature before eleven, and at eleven I answered everything at once without losing my thread. So far nobody has needed to call.

qa.a: Jagdish reads messages at eleven and at four.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel in the first days of the new rule?
qa.a: Jagdish felt restless and itchy in the first days, wanting to check the chat all the time.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do so that urgent matters still get through?
qa.a: Jagdish could make sure the team knows which matters count as urgent and how to call, as agreed with Indu.

qa.q: How might Indu feel about the change?
qa.a: Indu might feel worried at first about urgent matters, and reassured by "Call me" as a clear route.

Team lead's note on Uday, month two

Uday joined us as a junior developer and at first answered every message the moment it arrived. His code reviews were full of small slips. Last week he came to me with a plan. He would check chat and email only at eleven and at four, keep the morning from nine to eleven for coding with notifications off, and put a status note up: "Coding till 11, message again if urgent." Bhupen, who sits next to him, was sceptical. This week Uday finished the search feature two days early, and his review had one comment instead of eleven. I've asked him to share his routine at Friday's stand-up.

qa.q: At what times does Uday check messages?
What might Uday have been feeling when he came with the plan?
qa.a: He probably felt frustrated with his slips and hopeful that protecting his mornings would help.

qa.q: What could Uday add so urgent issues aren't missed?
qa.a: Keep the status note that invites a second message if urgent, or give the team lead a way to call during coding time.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Uday's routine now?
qa.a: Bhupen was sceptical at first, but after the early search feature he may be impressed and curious to try it.

grounding: A developer checks messages at fixed times and keeps the morning free for coding, so he is not interrupted all day.

passage:
Tuesday

Day four of the new rule and I actually wrote code this morning. Real code, two hours of it. Until last week I'd be halfway through a function and the chat would ping, and I'd answer, and then spend ten minutes finding where I was. Omkar said I looked like a startled pigeon every time my phone buzzed. So now: notifications off from nine. I check messages at eleven and at four, and I answer everything in one go. I put a line in my status, "Deep work till 11, call if on fire." Nobody called. Today I finished the login fix before lunch. At eleven there were fourteen messages. Not one was urgent. Honestly, that's the biggest surprise. I'm Raghav and I have been a pigeon too long.

qa.q: How many messages were waiting at eleven?
How did Raghav feel about what the fourteen messages turned out to be?
qa.a: That not one of the fourteen messages was urgent; Raghav felt relieved and a bit amused by it.

qa.q: What else could Raghav try to keep this working?
qa.a: Tell the team the two check times so they know when to expect replies, and keep the call-if-on-fire line.

qa.q: How might Omkar see the change?
qa.a: Omkar probably finds it funny and good, seeing Raghav calmer and no longer jumping at every buzz.

grounding: A developer checks messages at fixed times and keeps the morning free for coding to avoid constant interruptions.
